clinicalPearls: Type 3 is the non-ocular variant of Stickler syndrome caused by dominant variants in COL11A2, the gene for the alpha-2 chain of type XI collagen.
Because COL11A2 is not expressed in the vitreous, this subtype characteristically spares the eye, so there is no vitreoretinopathy or high myopia and no retinal-detachment risk.
The distinguishing feature is the combination of sensorineural or mixed deafness, midface hypoplasia with cleft palate, and early-onset osteoarthritis without ocular disease.
Hearing loss is typically more consistent and often more pronounced than in the ocular subtypes and warrants early audiological follow-up.
Facial features overlap with other Sticklers: a flat midface, depressed nasal bridge and Pierre Robin sequence with micrognathia, cleft palate and glossoptosis in infancy.
Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with mild vertebral flattening and premature joint degeneration produces stiffness and pain from early adulthood.
It is allelic and phenotypically overlapping with otospondylomegaepiphyseal dysplasia, which arises from recessive COL11A2 variants.
Distinguishing type 3 from the ocular types 1 and 2 is clinically important because retinal-detachment surveillance is not required.
reference.pathophysiology: Stickler syndrome type 3 is an autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in COL11A2, which encodes the alpha-2(XI) chain of type XI collagen, a minor fibrillar collagen that co-assembles with type II and type XI alpha-1 chains to regulate the diameter and spacing of type II collagen fibrils in cartilage and other tissues. Abnormal or reduced alpha-2(XI) chains disrupt the fibrillar collagen network of cartilage, the cartilaginous growth plate and the inner ear, producing spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, midfacial and palatal hypoplasia, and cochlear dysfunction with sensorineural or mixed hearing loss. Crucially, the vitreous humour of the eye assembles its type XI collagen using the alpha-2(V) chain of COL5A2 in place of alpha-2(XI), so COL11A2 is not required for normal vitreous architecture; this molecular substitution explains why type 3 disease, unlike the COL2A1-related type 1 and COL11A1-related type 2 forms, has a normal vitreous and does not confer the myopia, membranous or beaded vitreous phenotype, or the high risk of giant retinal tears and detachment that dominate the ocular subtypes. Dominant-negative and haploinsufficiency mechanisms both contribute, and the same gene produces a recessive, more severe skeletal-auditory phenotype when both alleles are affected.
additionalDifferentials: Stickler syndrome type 1 (COL2A1) with membranous vitreous and retinal detachment
Stickler syndrome type 2 (COL11A1) with beaded vitreous and ocular involvement
Otospondylomegaepiphyseal dysplasia from recessive COL11A2 variants
Marshall syndrome with ectodermal features and hearing loss
Kniest and other type II collagenopathies with skeletal dysplasia
Isolated Pierre Robin sequence or non-syndromic cleft palate

additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of COL11A2 with analysis of COL2A1 and COL11A1 to subtype Stickler syndrome
Comprehensive audiometry and brainstem-evoked response testing
Skeletal survey and spine imaging for spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia
Dilated ophthalmological examination to confirm the expected absence of vitreoretinopathy
Cleft-palate and airway assessment in infants with Pierre Robin sequence
Joint imaging to document early osteoarthritis
Family evaluation and pedigree analysis for dominant inheritance
redFlags: Neonatal airway obstruction from Pierre Robin sequence with micrognathia and glossoptosis
Feeding difficulty and aspiration associated with an unrepaired cleft palate
Progressive hearing loss impairing speech and language development
Disabling early joint pain suggesting advanced premature osteoarthritis
Recurrent otitis media with effusion compounding the sensorineural deficit
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; the main burdens are progressive hearing loss and early osteoarthritis, and because the vitreous is spared the sight-threatening retinal complications of the ocular subtypes do not occur, so long-term outcome is generally more favourable for vision than in types 1 and 2.
pitfalls: Labelling a child as ocular Stickler and imposing unnecessary retinal surveillance when the genotype is COL11A2
Conversely, withholding retinal surveillance before the subtype has been confirmed molecularly
Overlooking sensorineural hearing loss because attention is focused on the palate or joints
Confusing dominant type 3 with the more severe recessive otospondylomegaepiphyseal dysplasia
Missing Pierre Robin sequence as an early presenting feature in the newborn period
management: Audiological rehabilitation with hearing aids, and cochlear implantation where appropriate, for the dominant sensorineural or mixed deafness
Regular audiological surveillance given the consistent and often pronounced progressive hearing loss
Manage early-onset osteoarthritis and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with analgesia, physiotherapy and joint protection
Cleft palate repair and airway management for Pierre Robin sequence in infancy
Confirmatory dilated ophthalmic assessment with reassurance that vitreoretinopathy and retinal-detachment risk are absent in this subtype
Genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal dominant COL11A2 variant
Multidisciplinary care across audiology, rheumatology/orthopaedics and clinical genetics
